cards.front: Why is b & 0xFF needed when converting a byte to an int?
cards.back: Because a byte is sign-extended to int — 0xFF masks off the sign bits, giving 0–255
cards.extra: Without the mask, -1 becomes 0xFFFFFFFF instead of 255. Every byte-array-to-hex routine depends on this.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::03 Data Types
cards.example:
byte b = -1;
System.out.println((int) b);    // -1: sign-extended to int
System.out.println(b & 0xFF);   // 255: mask off the sign bits, 0..255

cards.front: What does System.console() give you that System.out does not?
cards.back: The ability to read input without echo (readPassword), and null when there is no terminal
cards.extra: It returns null in an IDE or when output is redirected — which is why password prompts must handle it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations
cards.example:
java.io.Console console = System.console();   // null when there is no terminal
if (console != null) {
    char[] password = console.readPassword("Password: ");   // read without echo
}
System.out.println(console == null ? "no terminal" : "terminal attached");

cards.front: What is headless mode?
cards.back: A JVM setting (java.awt.headless=true) that forbids creating windows, for servers with no display
cards.extra: AWT/Swing classes still load, but any attempt to show a frame throws HeadlessException.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools
cards.example:
System.setProperty("java.awt.headless", "true");
System.out.println(java.awt.GraphicsEnvironment.isHeadless());   // true: no display
try { new java.awt.Frame(); } catch (java.awt.HeadlessException e) { System.out.println("no windows: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()); }

cards.front: How do you detect the operating system in Java?
cards.back: System.getProperty("os.name"), usually with File.separator for path differences
cards.extra: os.version and os.arch complete the picture; there is no enum of operating systems in the JDK.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools
cards.example:
System.out.println(System.getProperty("os.name"));   // e.g. Windows 11 / Linux
System.out.println(java.io.File.separator);           // path differences between OSes

cards.front: What is "sneaky throws"?
cards.back: Throwing a checked exception from a method that does not declare it, via a generic cast trick
cards.extra: static <T extends Throwable> void sneakyThrow(Throwable t) throws T defeats the compiler's check; the JVM does not verify declared exceptions.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::00 Overview
cards.example:
class Sneaky {
    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    static  void sneakyThrow(Throwable t) throws E { throw (E) t; }
    void run() { sneakyThrow(new java.io.IOException("checked, but run() declares none")); }
}

cards.front: How do you turn a stack trace into a String?
cards.back: StringWriter sw = new StringWriter(); e.printStackTrace(new PrintWriter(sw));
cards.extra: That is the only reliable way to capture it; getStackTrace() gives frames, not the formatted text.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling
cards.example:
Exception e = new Exception("boom");
java.io.StringWriter sw = new java.io.StringWriter();
e.printStackTrace(new java.io.PrintWriter(sw));
System.out.println(sw.toString().contains("boom"));   // whole trace as a String

cards.front: What causes NoSuchFieldError?
cards.back: A field that existed at compile time is missing or renamed at run time — a binary compatibility break
cards.extra: Nothing in the source is wrong. Rebuild everything against the same version of the dependency.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What causes AbstractMethodError?
cards.back: A concrete class was compiled against an older interface that did not have the method, then ran against the newer one
cards.extra: The class never implemented the method because it did not exist when the class was compiled.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals
cards.example:
try {
    throw new AbstractMethodError("interface gained a method after compilation");
} catch (AbstractMethodError e) {
    System.out.println("concrete class was compiled against the older interface: " + e.getMessage());
}

cards.front: What causes IllegalAccessError?
cards.back: A member's access changed after compilation — for example a public method became private
cards.extra: Like the other linkage errors, it means the compiled code and the loaded class disagree.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals
cards.example:
try {
    throw new IllegalAccessError("compiled against a public method, now private");
} catch (IllegalAccessError e) {
    System.out.println("member access changed after compilation: " + e.getMessage());
}

cards.front: What does ExceptionInInitializerError wrap?
cards.back: The exception thrown by a static initializer — the class failed to initialise
cards.extra: The class is then unusable; the original cause is in getCause(), and the first failure is what matters.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What does "cannot find symbol" always mean?
cards.back: The compiler cannot resolve a name: a typo, a missing import, or the wrong scope
cards.extra: Read the symbol it names — variable, method or class — and the line number; the cause is always a naming problem.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::02 Basic Syntax
cards.example:
javac Missing.java
Missing.java:3: error: cannot find symbol
  Strng s = "x";   // typo (or a missing import / wrong scope)
        ^

cards.front: What is doclint?
cards.back: Javadoc's built-in validator for malformed HTML and invalid tags, on by default
cards.extra: It fails builds on things like an unclosed <p>. Disable selectively with -Xdoclint:none.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::12 Documentation::02 Javadoc
cards.example:
javadoc -Xdoclint:all MyClass.java   # default since Java 8: checks HTML and tags
javadoc -Xdoclint:none MyClass.java  # turn the checks off

cards.front: What is a synthetic member?
cards.back: One the compiler generates — e.g. this$0 for an inner class, or access$000 for private access
cards.extra: They are marked with the ACC_SYNTHETIC flag and mostly invisible to reflection unless you ask for them.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: Why is double-brace initialization an anti-pattern?
cards.back: new HashMap<>() {{ put(...); }} creates an anonymous subclass plus an instance initializer
cards.extra: It costs a class per use, breaks serialization and equality assumptions, and is opaque to readers.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects
cards.example:
java.util.Map dd = new java.util.HashMap<>() {{ put("a", 1); }};   // anonymous subclass + instance initializer
System.out.println(dd.getClass().getSuperclass().getSimpleName() + " anonymous=" + dd.getClass().isAnonymousClass());
java.util.Map plain = new java.util.HashMap<>(); plain.put("a", 1);

cards.front: What is the difference between Objects.hash and Objects.hashCode?
cards.back: Objects.hash(a, b) builds a combined hash from several values; Objects.hashCode(o) hashes one
cards.extra: Objects.hash allocates and varargs-boxes, so it is fine in equals/hashCode but not in hot loops.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects
cards.example:
String a = "a", b = "b";
System.out.println(java.util.Objects.hash(a, b));    // combined hash of several values
System.out.println(java.util.Objects.hashCode(a));   // one value
System.out.println(java.util.Objects.hashCode(a) == a.hashCode());

cards.front: What does the StackWalker API (Java 9) add over Thread.getStackTrace()?
cards.back: Lazy, streaming access to stack frames, with options to skip frames and keep class references
cards.extra: getStackTrace() materialises the whole array; StackWalker can stop after the frame it needs.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals
cards.example:
java.lang.StackWalker walker = java.lang.StackWalker.getInstance(java.lang.StackWalker.Option.RETAIN_CLASS_REFERENCE);
walker.walk(s -> { s.skip(1).limit(2).forEach(f -> System.out.println(f.getMethodName() + "@" + f.getDeclaringClass().getSimpleName())); return 0; });
System.out.println(new Throwable().getStackTrace().length);   // eager array vs lazy stream

cards.front: What is the System.Logger API?
cards.back: A platform logging facade in java.lang that delegates to whatever logging framework is present
cards.extra: Libraries can log without depending on SLF4J; the JDK routes it to java.util.logging by default.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::11 Logging::01 Logging Frameworks
cards.example:
System.Logger logger = System.getLogger("demo");   // java.lang platform facade
logger.log(System.Logger.Level.INFO, "delegates to whatever logging framework is present");
System.out.println(logger.getClass().getName());

cards.front: Which methods did Objects gain in Java 9?
cards.back: requireNonNullElse, requireNonNullElseGet, checkIndex, checkFromToIndex, checkFromIndexSize
cards.extra: The check methods throw IndexOutOfBoundsException with a useful message — ideal for Collections implementations.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects
cards.example:
System.out.println(java.util.Objects.requireNonNullElse(null, "fallback"));
System.out.println(java.util.Objects.requireNonNullElseGet(null, () -> "made"));
System.out.println(java.util.Objects.checkIndex(3, 5) + " " + java.util.Objects.checkFromToIndex(1, 3, 5) + " " + java.util.Objects.checkFromIndexSize(1, 2, 5));

cards.front: What is var in Java 10?
cards.back: Local variable type inference — the compiler infers the type from the initialiser; it is still static typing
cards.extra: It is not dynamic typing and cannot be used for fields, parameters, return types or without an initialiser.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::03 Data Types

cards.front: What did Java 11 standardise for HTTP?
cards.back: The new java.net.http.HttpClient, replacing HttpURLConnection for new code
cards.extra: It supports HTTP/2, WebSocket and async calls with CompletableFuture.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::03 Networking in Java
cards.example:
java.net.http.HttpClient client = java.net.http.HttpClient.newHttpClient();   // Java 11 API
java.net.http.HttpRequest request = java.net.http.HttpRequest.newBuilder(java.net.URI.create("https://example.com")).GET().build();
System.out.println(client.getClass().getSimpleName() + " " + request.method());   // not HttpURLConnection

cards.front: How do preview features work?
cards.back: They ship in a release but require --enable-preview, and they expire in the next release
cards.extra: Code using them is not future-proof: it must be recompiled and may change before standardisation.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::00 Overview

cards.front: What rule applies to var in lambda parameters?
cards.back: Either all parameters use var or none do — mixing is a compile error
cards.extra: It exists so annotations can be applied to lambda parameters: (@NonNull var x) -> ....
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::01 Functional Interfaces
cards.example:
java.util.function.BiFunction ok = (var a, var b) -> a + b;   // all var
java.util.function.BiFunction plain = (a, b) -> a + b;         // none
// (var a, Integer b) -> a + b   // mixing is a compile error
System.out.println(ok.apply(1, 2) + " " + plain.apply(3, 4));

cards.front: How do constructors delegate to each other?
cards.back: With this(...) as the first statement, so one constructor does the real work
cards.extra: A constructor cannot call both this() and super() — only one, and only first.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects
cards.example:
class Point {
    int x, y;
    Point() { this(0, 0); }   // this(...) must be the first statement
    Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }   // one constructor does the work
}

cards.front: What is a copy constructor?
cards.back: A constructor that takes an instance of the same type and copies its state
cards.extra: It gives you control over shallow vs deep copying, which clone() does not.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects
cards.example:
class Point {
    int x, y;
    Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
    Point(Point other) { this(other.x, other.y); }   // same type: copies its state
    static void run() { Point a = new Point(1, 2); Point b = new Point(a); System.out.println(b.x + "," + b.y + " " + (a != b)); }
}

cards.front: What is a lossy conversion in Java?
cards.back: A narrowing conversion that can lose information — long to int, double to float
cards.extra: Java requires an explicit cast for it, and the compiler warns when the value clearly does not fit.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::03 Data Types
cards.example:
long big = 1_000_000_000L;
int narrow = (int) big;   // narrowing: can lose information
double d = 1.9;
float f = (float) d;      // narrowing: precision loss
System.out.println(narrow + " " + f);

cards.front: Why does byte b = 1; b += 1; compile while b = b + 1; does not?
cards.back: Compound assignment operators contain an implicit cast back to the left-hand type
cards.extra: That is why i += 1.5 on an int compiles and silently truncates.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::03 Data Types
cards.example:
byte b = 1;
b += 1;   // compiles: implicit cast back to byte
// b = b + 1;   // error: int result cannot be assigned to byte
System.out.println(b);

cards.front: What does the xor operator do on booleans versus integers?
cards.back: On booleans it is true when exactly one operand is true; on integers it is a bitwise exclusive or
cards.extra: There is no short-circuit version of xor — both operands are always evaluated.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::03 Data Types
cards.example:
boolean a = true, b = false;
System.out.println(a ^ b);   // true: exactly one boolean operand is true
System.out.println(5 ^ 3);   // 6: 0101 ^ 0011 = 0110, bitwise exclusive or

cards.front: What is bit masking used for?
cards.back: Isolating, setting or clearing specific bits with AND, OR and XOR against a mask
cards.extra: n | (1 << k) sets bit k, n & ~(1 << k) clears it, (n >> k) & 1 reads it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::03 Data Types
cards.example:
int flags = 0b0000_1010;
System.out.println(flags & 0b0000_0010);   // isolate bit 1 -> 2
System.out.println(flags | 0b0000_0101);   // set bits -> 15
System.out.println(flags ^ 0b0000_1010);   // toggle bits -> 0

cards.front: What must compareTo return?
cards.back: A negative, zero or positive int — only the sign is specified, never the magnitude
cards.extra: Returning a difference can overflow: a - b on large ints gives the wrong sign. Use Integer.compare.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects
cards.example:
Integer a = 3, b = 5;
System.out.println(a.compareTo(b));   // negative: only the sign is specified
System.out.println(b.compareTo(a));   // positive
System.out.println(a.compareTo(3));   // zero

cards.front: What is a covariant return type?
cards.back: An override may return a subtype of the superclass's return type
cards.extra: It is why clone() can be declared to return the concrete type, and why builders return their own class.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::12 Inheritance
cards.example:
class Parent { Parent make() { return this; } }
class Sub extends Parent { @Override Sub make() { return this; } }   // subtype return type
// A method with the same signature and a different return type alone cannot override.

cards.front: What does "effectively final" mean?
cards.back: A variable that is never reassigned after initialisation, even without the final keyword
cards.extra: Java 8 requires it for lambda and anonymous-class capture, which is why the compiler complains about reassigned locals.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::00 Overview
cards.example:
int x = 1;                                    // effectively final without the keyword
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println(x);     // OK: never reassigned
// x = 2;   // would not compile: no longer effectively final
r.run();

cards.front: What is an unchecked cast warning?
cards.back: The compiler cannot prove the cast is type-safe, because generics are erased at runtime
cards.extra: (List<String>) obj compiles with a warning; the cast is only checked at the raw type level.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::04 Collections::09 Generics
cards.example:
java.util.List items = new java.util.ArrayList();
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")   // compiler cannot prove the cast: generics are erased
java.util.List strings = (java.util.List) items;
System.out.println(strings);

cards.front: In what order are static variables initialised?
cards.back: In text order, along with static blocks, after the class is loaded
cards.extra: A static initialiser that reads a field declared below it sees the default value.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::04 Static Keyword
cards.example:
class Order {
    static int a = 1;   // initialised in text order along with static blocks
    static { a = 2; }
    static int b = a + 1;
    static void show() { System.out.println(a + " " + b); }   // 2 3
}

cards.front: Is the return type part of a method's signature?
cards.back: No — the signature is name plus parameter types only
cards.extra: That is why you cannot overload on return type alone: int f() and String f() clash.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::02 Attributes and Methods
cards.example:
class Base { Object f() { return "x"; } }
class Sub extends Base { @Override String f() { return "y"; } }   // same name + params: the return type is not in the signature
// long f() would not be an overload: same signature, different return type

cards.front: What does Externalizable do better than Serializable?
cards.back: You write the state yourself in writeExternal/readExternal, so it is faster and smaller — and needs a public no-arg constructor
cards.extra: Serializable serialises the whole graph reflectively; Externalizable serialises exactly what you choose.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::17 Serialization
cards.example:
class Data implements java.io.Externalizable {
    int value;
    public Data() {}   // public no-arg constructor required
    public void writeExternal(java.io.ObjectOutput out) throws java.io.IOException { out.writeInt(value); }
    public void readExternal(java.io.ObjectInput in) throws java.io.IOException, ClassNotFoundException { value = in.readInt(); }
}

cards.front: What is serialVersionUID for?
cards.back: A version stamp: if the receiver's value differs from the sender's, deserialization fails with InvalidClassException
cards.extra: Declare it explicitly — the computed default changes whenever the class's shape changes, silently breaking compatibility.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::17 Serialization
cards.example:
class User implements java.io.Serializable {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;   // version stamp
    int id;
}
// A different value on the receiver side makes deserialization fail with InvalidClassException

cards.front: What does transient do?
cards.back: Excludes a field from default serialization
cards.extra: The field is restored as its default value (null/0) on deserialization, so any invariant involving it must be re-established in readObject.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::17 Serialization

cards.front: What is the difference between || and | on booleans?
cards.back: || short-circuits (right side skipped when left is true); | always evaluates both
cards.extra: Use || for conditions; the eager form is only right when both sides must run for side effects.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::04 Conditionals
cards.example:
class Probe {
    boolean hit(String tag) { System.out.println(tag); return true; }
    static void run() { Probe p = new Probe(); boolean s = true || p.hit("skipped"); boolean e = true | p.hit("evaluated"); }
}   // || skips the right side; | evaluates both

cards.front: Why is catch (Throwable t) bad practice?
cards.back: It swallows Error too — OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError — which the JVM cannot recover from
cards.extra: Catch Exception for recoverable failures, and let Errors propagate.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling
cards.example:
try {
    throw new OutOfMemoryError("simulated");   // an Error, not an Exception
} catch (Throwable t) {
    System.out.println("swallowed " + t.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": JVM cannot recover");
}

cards.front: What is a suppressed exception?
cards.back: An exception attached to another (via addSuppressed) instead of replacing it
cards.extra: try-with-resources does this automatically: the body's exception is primary and the close() failure is suppressed.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: When should you wrap an exception rather than rethrow it?
cards.back: Wrap when the failure must be expressed in your abstraction's terms; rethrow when the caller can act on the original
cards.extra: Always pass the cause — wrapping without it destroys the stack trace that explains the failure.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling
cards.example:
class Service {
    void load() throws java.io.IOException { throw new java.io.IOException("disk"); }
    void wrap() { try { load(); } catch (java.io.IOException e) { throw new IllegalStateException("load failed", e); } }   // your abstraction's terms
    void rethrow() throws java.io.IOException { load(); }   // caller can act on the original
}

cards.front: Why does reflective invocation throw InvocationTargetException?
cards.back: It wraps whatever the target method threw, so the reflective call itself never appears to throw it
cards.extra: Call getCause() to get the real exception; forgetting this is the classic reflection debugging trap.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::22 Reflection
cards.example:
try {
    Integer.class.getMethod("parseInt", String.class).invoke(null, "not a number");
} catch (java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException e) {
    System.out.println("wrapped: " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName());   // NumberFormatException
} catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) { System.out.println("method lookup failed"); }

cards.front: Does the compiler validate @SuppressWarnings values?
cards.back: No — unknown names are ignored silently, and each IDE understands its own set
cards.extra: unchecked, rawtypes and deprecation are the portable ones; a typo simply suppresses nothing.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::02 Annotations
cards.example:
class Suppress {
    @SuppressWarnings("made.up.key")   // unknown name is ignored silently
    void f() { java.util.List raw = new java.util.ArrayList(); }
}

cards.front: Does Java have a built-in Pair class?
cards.back: No — the JDK offers Map.Entry, AbstractMap.SimpleEntry, or your own record
cards.extra: A record record Pair<A, B>(A first, B second) {} is clearer than a framework tuple, which has no names.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects
cards.example:
java.util.Map.Entry e = new java.util.AbstractMap.SimpleEntry<>("a", 1);
System.out.println(e.getKey() + "=" + e.getValue());   // no java.util.Pair in the JDK: Map.Entry or your own record

cards.front: Should a method return null instead of an empty Optional?
cards.back: Never — an Optional-returning method must always return a real Optional
cards.extra: Returning null breaks the entire point of the type and produces NPEs where the caller expected empty().
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::04 Collections::10 Optionals
cards.example:
class Lookup {
    java.util.Optional find(boolean present) {
        return present ? java.util.Optional.of("value") : java.util.Optional.empty();   // always a real Optional, never null
    }
}

cards.front: How do you get the name of the currently executing method?
cards.back: StackWalker (Java 9) or new Throwable().getStackTrace()[0] — there is no direct API
cards.extra: Both are approximations: the JIT may inline, and reflection/ lambdas change the frame name.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals
cards.example:
String name = java.lang.StackWalker.getInstance().walk(s -> s.findFirst().get().getMethodName());
System.out.println(name);   // m: the currently executing method
System.out.println(new Throwable().getStackTrace()[0].getMethodName());   // m too
